accroche: An unfinished task is said to stay in memory better than a finished one. A 2025 meta-analysis does not find it.
contenu_vulgarise:
According to the most widespread account, probably embellished over time, the psychologist Kurt Lewin supposedly once noticed that a café waiter remembered in detail the orders not yet paid at his tables, but forgot within minutes those he had just settled. The psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik supposedly drew from this the experiments that would give the effect its name.

## The Mechanism

In 1927, Zeigarnik publishes in German, in the journal *Psychologische Forschung*, the study that will give the effect its name: interrupted tasks are said to be better retained than tasks carried through to completion.

The explanation put forward comes from Lewin's field theory: starting a task creates a tension specific to that task, which makes its content more accessible in memory; it relaxes when the task is completed and persists when it is interrupted. The idea has had an immense career outside the laboratory: TV series cliffhangers, notifications that cut a piece of information in two, to-do lists we keep in view so as not to forget them.

## What This Shifts

In 2025, Romain Ghibellini and Beat Meier publish in *Humanities and Social Sciences Communications* a meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects. Their conclusion: they find no memory advantage for unfinished tasks, an effect the authors describe as particularly hard to replicate. Nearly a century of citations has not been enough to consolidate what the original experiment reported. The authors suggest that the effect may depend on circumstances such as the experimenter's authority, the demands of the situation, or involvement in the task, more common in the past than today, which would explain the difficulty of replicating it.

What holds up, on the other hand, is a neighboring effect, studied in 1928 by Maria Ovsiankina: an interrupted task creates the need to resume it, even with no reward at stake. Ghibellini and Meier find a general tendency to resume interrupted tasks, the Ovsiankina effect, where the memory advantage is not borne out.

The shift is precise: what is remembered of Zeigarnik's name, remembering the unfinished better, does not withstand this meta-analysis. What holds is wanting to go back to it: a desire to resume, not a more faithful memory. Cliffhangers probably work very well; the reason attributed to them for a century is probably not the right one.

repere.texte: A meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects finds no memory advantage for unfinished tasks, but a general tendency to resume interrupted tasks.
repere.source: Ghibellini & Meier, “Interruption, Recall and Resumption: A Meta-Analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina Effects,” Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 2025

carte.punch: We do not remember better what we left unfinished. We just want to go back to it.
carte.idee: The Zeigarnik effect, popularized since 1927, holds that an interrupted task stays in memory better than a finished one. A 2025 meta-analysis does not find this memory advantage, but a general tendency to resume what we left in suspense.

quiz.question: What does the 2025 meta-analysis conclude about the Zeigarnik effect and the Ovsiankina effect?
choix: That both effects are confirmed identically in all the studies surveyed
That neither effect withstands examination of the replication attempts
That the memory advantage for the unfinished does not hold, but the tendency to resume an interrupted task is confirmed
That only manual tasks, and not intellectual ones, produce a memory effect
quiz.explication: Ghibellini and Meier find no memory advantage for unfinished tasks: the Zeigarnik effect has no universal validity. They do, however, find a general tendency to resume interrupted tasks, the Ovsiankina effect.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the name of the Zeigarnik effect come from?
choix: From an experiment run by Maria Ovsiankina in 1928 on the resumption of interrupted tasks
From a study published in 1927 by Bluma Zeigarnik, inspired by an observation by Kurt Lewin about a café waiter
From a 2025 survey that invalidates all effects related to unfinished tasks
From a protocol run on psychiatric patients in the 1950s
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Zeigarnik publishes in 1927 the study that gives the effect its name, based on an observation attributed to Lewin about a waiter who remembered unpaid orders better.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does the Ghibellini and Meier (2025) meta-analysis measure for the Ovsiankina effect?
choix: A total absence of tendency to resume interrupted tasks
A rate of resumption of interrupted tasks below the chance level
A memory advantage for unfinished tasks confirmed in half of the studies
Resumption of interrupted tasks about 67% of the time, clearly above the 50% chance level
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The meta-analysis puts the resumption of interrupted tasks at about 67% of the time, well above the chance level set at 50%, which confirms the Ovsiankina effect.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many publications does the Ghibellini and Meier (2025) meta-analysis cover?
choix: Fifty-nine publications, thirty-eight on the Zeigarnik effect and twenty on the Ovsiankina effect
Fifty-nine publications, all devoted exclusively to the Zeigarnik effect
A single study, Zeigarnik's, published in 1927
Thirteen publications, selected from the most cited since 1927
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The meta-analysis pools fifty-nine publications, thirty-eight on the Zeigarnik effect, twenty on the Ovsiankina effect, and one on both at once.
